transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my wife actually made the appointment for me, but I guess I'm here because... I don't know, nothing feels like mine anymore. It's hard to explain. Like, I used to be this guy who was always into something, you know? I'd get so excited about things. I used to paint these big murals, just pouring hours into them on my days off. And I loved running, just getting out there and clearing my head. I'd play basketball with the guys on weekends, and even at work—I've been a bartender for years—I used to get a real kick out of making a really good drink, you know, getting the mix just right and seeing someone enjoy it. But now... now I just stand there. Behind the bar, at home, wherever. I just stand there like I don't care about any of it. The guys will call about a game, and I just look at the phone. I look at my paints and they just look like garbage. It's like someone flipped a switch and drained all the color and the... the point out of everything. I just don't care. About anything. And it's not just a bad day, it's every day. I just wake up and I'm already tired of it all, and I don't even want to try to do the things I used to love because I know I'm just going to feel nothing anyway.
How long have you been feeling this way, like nothing matters and you don't care about the things you used to enjoy?

Well, it’s... it’s been a while now. I’d say about two months. Yeah, two months exactly, almost to the day, actually. It started right around the time the bar got bought out. You see, I’d been working there for, gosh, almost fifteen years, and I had things set up just the way I liked them. I had my regulars, I knew exactly what they drank before they even sat down, I had the inventory system down to a science... I mean, I really built that place up, in my own way. And then these new guys come in, some corporate hospitality group, and they just... they changed everything. They brought in these new menus, got rid of all the local craft beers I spent years sourcing, changed the lighting, even made us wear these ridiculous uniforms. It was like everything I had been working toward, all that effort and pride, they just wiped it out overnight. And that’s when it started, this... this feeling. I remember the first week they took over, I came home and my wife asked how it went, and I just sat on the couch and stared at the wall. I didn't even want to take my shoes off. And it’s just been like that ever since. Two whole months of just waking up, going to that place that doesn't even feel like mine anymore, coming home, and feeling absolutely nothing about any of it. Just two months of... nothing.
Do you still enjoy things like eating or spending time with your wife, or has the feeling of not caring affected those areas of your life as well?

Well, honestly... I don't really enjoy eating either. It's like food is just another chore now, you know? My wife, she tries, she really does. She'll make my favorite things—like she made this pot roast last Sunday, the one with the little potatoes and carrots that she cooks all day so the house smells amazing. Normally, I'd be all over that, stealing pieces of potato before it's even done. But she put the plate down in front of me, and I just looked at it. It could have been cardboard. I took maybe two bites just so she wouldn't look so sad, but it tasted like dust. 

And at work... man, at work it's even worse. I used to grab a burger from the kitchen on my break, sit and shoot the breeze with the line cooks. Now, most days I completely forget to eat. I won't even realize I haven't had anything until it's like 10 PM and I'm pouring a drink and my hands start shaking so bad I can barely hold the jigger. The glass is rattling against the shaker, and I'm just thinking, 'Right, I haven't eaten since yesterday morning.' And even then, I don't want anything. I'll wait until closing, when everyone's gone and I'm wiping down the mats, and I might grab a few bites of some cold fries or a leftover piece of flatbread from the back. But honestly, even just looking at it makes me feel sick to my stomach. I just chew it because I know I have to, not because I want it. 

And as for spending time with my wife... I mean, I love her, I do. But sitting on the couch watching TV with her used to be relaxing. Now I'm just sitting there, physically next to her, but I'm a million miles away, just trapped in this heavy, gray fog. I can tell it hurts her feelings that I'm so checked out, which makes me feel guilty, but even the guilt is just... dull. Everything is just so dull.
Have you had any thoughts about not wanting to live or hurting yourself since you started feeling this way?

No, no, I haven't... I haven't thought about hurting myself or anything like that. I mean, it's not like I want to die, you know? It's more just... I don't really care about living. If that makes any sense. Like, if a bus was coming at me, I don't know if I'd jump out of the way, but I'm not going to go looking for the bus. 

I just... I think about how tired I am. Like, bone-tired. The kind of tired where even breathing feels like it takes too much effort. I remember the other night, I was closing up the bar, and I was just staring at the mop bucket. Just staring at this dirty, gray water, and I thought, "This is it. This is exactly how my life feels." Just this murky, stagnant thing that I'm dragging around. And I stood there for maybe twenty minutes, just looking at it, because the idea of actually lifting the mop and pushing it across the floor seemed impossible. It wasn't that I wanted to end it all right there, I just wanted to stop. I wanted everything to just... pause. 

My wife, she gets so worried. She'll ask me if I'm okay, and I always say yes, because what else am I supposed to say? "No, honey, I feel like a ghost in my own life"? I don't want to put that on her. She's already dealing with enough, seeing me like this. But no, to answer your question, I haven't made any plans or had thoughts of doing something to myself. It's just this heavy, heavy emptiness that makes me wish I could just go to sleep and not have to wake up and do it all over again. But I wouldn't actually do anything to make that happen. I just... I just endure it, I guess. That's all I'm doing right now. Just enduring.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since you started feeling this way?

Sleep? Yeah, sleep is... it's a whole other mess right now. You'd think, being as exhausted as I am, like I was just saying, that I'd just hit the pillow and pass out, right? But it doesn't work like that. Not anymore. I'll get home from the bar, usually around 2:30 or 3:00 in the morning, and I am dead on my feet. My legs ache, my back aches from standing on those hard mats all night, and my eyes are practically burning. So I'll do my routine, you know, brush my teeth, try not to wake my wife—she's usually dead to the world by then—and I'll crawl into bed. 

And the second my head hits the pillow, it's like a switch flips in my brain. Suddenly, I'm not tired anymore. Well, my body is, but my mind just starts racing. It's like a projector clicking on, showing a highlight reel of everything that went wrong that day, or just every mistake I've ever made. I'll lie there staring at the ceiling fan, thinking about how I rang in the wrong vodka for table four, or how I didn't push back when the new manager told me to reorganize the speed rail in a way that makes absolutely no sense for pouring efficiency. I'll just stew on it. I'll play out these arguments in my head that I never actually had, thinking of what I should have said to defend my way of doing things. 

And this goes on for hours. I'll watch the digital clock on the nightstand just flip, minute by minute. 3:45... 4:12... 4:30. And the longer I'm awake, the more anxious I get about not sleeping, which of course makes it even harder to sleep. I'll toss and turn, try to get comfortable, try to clear my head, but it's just this constant loop of thoughts. 

Then, finally, I don't even know when, I'll drift off. But it's not a good, deep sleep. It's that light, fitful kind where you feel like you're still half awake the whole time. And it never lasts. Without fail, I'll pop awake around four or five in the afternoon—because, you know, my schedule is all shifted from the bar—and that's it. I'm up. I'll try to force myself back to sleep, because I know I only got maybe three or four hours, but it's useless. I'll just lie there, feeling completely drained, but totally unable to shut my brain off again. So I just end up getting out of bed, wandering around the house in a daze, dreading having to go back to work and do it all over again on almost no rest. It's torturous, really. It just makes the whole gray fog feeling that much thicker during the day.
Have you noticed yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

Moving slower? No... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, I know I just told you how bone-tired I am all the time, and I definitely am, but when it comes to actually moving my body... no, it still does what it's supposed to do at the normal speed. 

You have to understand, behind a bar, muscle memory just kind of takes over. Like, take last night for example. We got this huge rush right around 11:30, a bunch of people coming in after the theater let out down the street, and suddenly I've got, I don't know, six or seven drink tickets printing all at once. I'm still grabbing the shaker tin, scooping the ice, pouring a four-count of gin with one hand while grabbing the vermouth with the other... it all happens just as fast as it always has. I'm not fumbling around or moving like I'm underwater or anything like that. Because if you move slow in this industry, you get eaten alive, you know? The servers will just stand there at the service well, tapping their pens on their trays, staring daggers at you if you hold up their tables. 

So my hands are still quick. I can still wipe down the whole rail in two seconds flat. And reacting... like, if a glass gets knocked off the bar mat, I'll still shoot my hand out and catch it before it shatters on the floor. I actually did that just on Tuesday. Some guy in a suit knocked over his empty highball glass, and boom, I caught it. Didn't even have to think about it. 

So, no, physically I'm not slow at all. It's just the... the desire to do any of it that's completely gone. The actual physical movement, my reflexes, my hands, they're all still firing right on time. It's actually kind of weird when you think about it, how your body can just keep running on autopilot, moving perfectly fast like a machine, even when your mind is just completely checked out and you feel like you're dragging a hundred pounds of lead. But yeah, to answer your question, no, I haven't noticed being physically slower.
Have you lost any weight since you started feeling this way?

Weight? Yeah... yeah, I've definitely dropped a few sizes. My work slacks are just kind of hanging off me right now. I actually had to take a pocket knife and punch a new hole in my belt last week just to keep them up. It's not like I'm trying to diet or anything like that, it's just... food doesn't even register for me anymore. 

Most days, I completely forget to eat. I'll get up in the late afternoon, have some black coffee, head to the bar, and I won't even realize my stomach is empty until my hands start shaking behind the bar. I'll be in the middle of a rush, trying to pour a steady stream from the speed pourer into a jigger, and my fingers will just be trembling. Not from nerves, just because my blood sugar has completely bottomed out and I'm running on absolute fumes. 

And you'd think that would be the cue to go grab a burger or something from the kitchen, right? But I just... I don't. I just push through the whole shift like that, ignoring the shakes. Then, after closing, when the doors are locked and the stools are up on the tables and it's just me doing the till, I might try to find something. I'll go into the back cooler and grab whatever the kitchen guys left behind. Usually it's just a few bites of something cold, like a leftover chicken strip or some soggy fries. But honestly, I'll take maybe one or two bites, and I just feel sick looking at it. My stomach just totally turns. The texture, the grease... it all just makes me nauseous. I end up just tossing it in the garbage. 

My wife, she tries, bless her. She'll try to make me a nice hot plate before my shift, but I just sit there at the kitchen table pushing the food around with my fork. I feel incredibly guilty because she cooked and she's worried about me getting too thin, but chewing just feels like so much work, and swallowing feels impossible. So, yeah, I'm definitely losing weight, because I'm basically just running on nothing but coffee and whatever cold scraps I can force down at 3 AM before I feel like throwing up.
Have you been feeling restless or fidgety since you started feeling this way?

Restless? No... no, I wouldn't say that. Fidgety isn't really the word I'd use for how I am right now. I mean, I see fidgety all the time at work, right? You get these guys sitting at the bar, and they're constantly peeling the wet labels off their beer bottles, or they're tapping their credit cards on the mahogany, bouncing their knees up and down against the brass rail... just all this nervous energy, especially the younger guys or people waiting on a date or something. I watch them do it all night. But me? I'm the exact opposite of that. 

If I have a free second—which, you know, isn't often, but if the floor clears out for a minute and I'm just standing by the service well—I don't tap my foot. I don't drum my fingers on the speed rack. I just... stand there. I'll lean my back against the cooler door and just stare at the rows of liquor bottles until everything kind of blurs together. It's like I don't even have the spare energy required to fidget. 

My wife actually mentioned something similar just the other day. We were sitting on the couch on my day off, supposedly watching some home improvement show she likes, and usually, in the old days, I'd be shifting around, maybe getting up to check the fridge, adjusting the pillows, whatever. But she looked over at me and said I was sitting so still I looked like a statue. And she was right. I was just planted there, staring at the TV without really watching it. My hands were just resting flat on my legs. 

It’s like... to be restless, you have to have some kind of spark in you, you know? Some kind of motor running that needs to burn off fuel. But my tank is just so completely empty. There's no extra energy to pace the floor or wring my hands. I'm just heavy. So, yeah, no, I'm not restless at all. If anything, I'm just... anchored to the floor until somebody needs a drink.
Do you often feel guilty about things you've done or haven't done since you started feeling this way?

Guilty? Yeah... God, yeah. It just absolutely eats at me, honestly. You have to understand, working in a place like mine for as long as I have, you don't just pour drinks. You become a sort of... I don't know, a fixture. A mentor, I guess. 

We get these kids, these younger bartenders coming in, just trying to learn the ropes. And I was supposed to be the guy showing them how to handle a Friday night rush without losing their minds, how to build a regular clientele, how to survive in this industry. And it wasn't just them, it was the neighborhood, too. We have this back room at the bar, right? Usually it's just used for overflow or private parties, but I had told all these local artists—these kids trying to get their stuff seen, musicians, painters—that they could use the space. I promised them. I looked them in the eye and said, "Yeah, I'll set it up with the owner, we'll get your art on the walls, we'll do a whole showcase night for you." 

But since I've been... since things got so heavy for me, I just completely dropped the ball. I didn't make the calls. I didn't set up the schedules. I just let it all slip away because I couldn't even bring myself to care. And now I just keep thinking about how I let down the younger bartenders who were looking up to me, and the artists I promised that space to. They were counting on me. That was their big chance, you know? In this city, getting a free space to show your work or having an older guy actually take the time to teach you the trade properly... it's huge. It can make or break you. 

And I just wrecked it. I wrecked their shot. I come into work now and I look at those empty walls in the back room, or I watch one of the new kids struggling to keep up with a rush because I haven't trained them right, and this overwhelming feeling just washes over me. It feels like I deserve whatever happens to me for wrecking their shot. Whatever bad luck, whatever misery comes my way... I completely deserve it. You don't just mess with people's dreams and their livelihoods like that. You don't make promises to kids who are hungry for a chance and then just pull the rug out from under them because you can't get your own head straight. It’s just... it's unforgivable, really. I ruined their chances, and I just feel like I'm finally getting exactly what I have coming to me.
Do you find yourself having trouble speaking or finding the right words when talking to people?

Trouble finding words? No... no, I wouldn't say that. 

See, when you've been working behind a mahogany bar for as long as I have, talking just becomes... it's like breathing. It's pure muscle memory. You learn exactly what to say and how to say it without even having to fire up your brain. Somebody sits down, throws a damp twenty on a coaster, you don't even have to think. You just hit 'em with the script. "What's your poison tonight?" "Rough day at the office?" "You want to keep this open or close it out?" It's all just burned into my vocal cords at this point. 

Now, don't get me wrong, I don't exactly *want* to talk these days. Like I was saying earlier about having absolutely no fuel in the tank? The actual desire to hold a conversation is completely gone. When I'm wiping down the speed rail at the end of the night, I'm not looking to shoot the breeze with the barbacks or the bouncers like I used to. I just want to be left alone with my thoughts, as heavy as they are. But if somebody asks me a question, or if a customer needs to be talked down because they've had one too many IPAs, I don't stumble. I don't sit there stuttering or forgetting the word for a highball glass or a muddler or a strainer. The vocabulary is all still right there. 

It's the same thing at home with my wife. She'll ask me about the electric bill, or if I want to try to go to the hardware store on my Sunday off, and I can give her a full, complete answer. I know the words. I might just say them in this flat, quiet voice, you know, just kind of monotone because I'm so damn worn out and carrying all that guilt I mentioned, but the words themselves? They haven't gone anywhere. I don't lose my train of thought mid-sentence or anything like that. I just... I just don't have anything good or hopeful to say anymore. But the actual mechanics of speaking, the ability to pull a sentence together? No, that hasn't changed a bit. I can still talk a regular's ear off if I need to play the part for a tip, it just takes every last ounce of whatever I have left to do it.
Have you noticed any changes in how quickly or slowly you think, compared to before you started feeling this way?

Yeah, I have. It's... it's honestly like my brain is trying to walk through wet concrete these days. Everything is just so incredibly slow. You know, I've been doing this job for a long time, and a lot of the mental work used to just be completely automatic for me. Take inventory, for example. I used to be able to walk into the liquor room with my clipboard, scan the shelves, and just knock it out in ten minutes flat. I knew exactly what we had, what we were moving, what we needed to order from the distributor before they even called. It was second nature. 

But now? I go back there to do the counts, and I just stand there staring at the bottles. I'll start counting the well vodka or the bourbons, and I'll get to maybe four or five, and then my mind just completely blanks. I'll lose count three times on the exact same shelf. I just lose the thread of what I'm doing. It's like the gears in my head are rusted shut. 

And it's not even just the big tasks like the weekly liquor order. It's the stupid, tiny things that really show me how bad it's gotten. When I'm setting up my station before a shift, you know, getting the fruit caddies ready... I'll just freeze trying to decide something incredibly simple, like what garnish to restock first. I'll be standing there looking at the cutting board, holding a paring knife, and I can't figure out if I should slice the limes or pull out the cocktail cherries. It's a choice that shouldn't take even a fraction of a second, but I'll just stand there, totally paralyzed, trying to force my brain to make a decision. The processing speed is just gone. I used to be so sharp, calculating tabs in my head, remembering a dozen drink orders at once, but now I can barely figure out how to restock a lemon without my brain just shutting down on me.
Do you feel like you're moving slower or more slowly than you used to, physically?

Physically? Moving slow... no, I wouldn't say that. It's funny you ask, because you'd think with my head being so bogged down and foggy like I was just saying, my body would naturally follow suit, but... no. It doesn't. 

That muscle memory I was talking about earlier with talking to customers? It applies to my feet and my hands, too. You see, behind a bar, especially a high-volume place like ours on a weekend, space is incredibly tight. You've got maybe three feet, tops, between the speed rail and the backbar coolers, and you're constantly weaving around the other bartender, the barbacks hauling ice, the waitresses coming up to the service well to grab their tickets. It's essentially a dance. The "bartender's shuffle," some of the old-timers call it. And I've been doing that exact dance for so many years that my body just inherently knows the tempo. Two steps left to the ice bin, pivot on the right foot, grab the shaker tin, reach down for the well rail... it's all entirely on physical autopilot. 

I can still sling drinks and wipe down the mahogany just as fast as I always have. I can still haul a fifty-pound keg from the walk-in cooler and tap it without missing a beat, or scrub down the three-compartment sink at the end of the night at my usual pace. It's actually a very strange, almost disconnected feeling, to be completely honest with you. My body is moving at its normal clip, my hands are shaking a margarita or pouring a draft just as quick as they did ten years ago, but inside? Inside, I feel like I'm completely hollowed out. 

But outwardly, physically... no, my wife hasn't mentioned me walking any slower around the house, and I certainly haven't noticed it taking me any longer to walk the four blocks from the train station to the front doors of the bar every afternoon. My legs and arms work at the exact same speed they always have. It's just... the engine running them is completely exhausted, you know? But the actual physical movement itself hasn't slowed down a bit.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling like you need to move around when you're sitting still?

Fidgeting? No, not at all. If anything, it’s the exact opposite. When I actually get a chance to sit down, I just stay there. Like a sack of wet sand. 

You know, in my line of work, you’re on your feet for eight, ten, twelve hours a shift on the hard rubber mats behind the bar. The only time I really get to sit is if I take a quick ten-minute breather out back by the dumpsters on an old plastic milk crate, or when I finally get home at three in the morning and collapse into the recliner in the living room. And when I hit that chair, I don't tap my foot. I don't bounce my knee or pick at my fingernails or pace around the room. I just sink into the cushions and stay completely still. 

My wife, she’ll be sitting on the sofa reading or watching her shows, and I’ll just be sitting there in the dark, staring at the wall next to the television. I don't feel any urge whatsoever to get up and move. I don't have that kind of nervous, jittery energy. Like I was saying before about the tank being completely empty... fidgeting takes energy, you know? It takes a kind of spark or a restlessness that I just absolutely do not have in me right now. 

I can sit at the kitchen table with a mug of coffee, completely zone out, and the coffee will go ice cold before I even shift my weight in the chair. I could sit in the exact same spot for hours without moving a single muscle, just letting all these heavy, awful thoughts I’ve been having just wash over me. So no, I don't get fidgety. When I stop moving, I just... stop completely.
Do you feel like you're a burden to your wife or others around you?

Yeah. Yeah, I do. All the time, honestly. It's... it's heavy. It's this weight I carry around with me, and it's not just about my wife, though I know I'm no picnic to live with right now, just sitting in that recliner like a lump like I told you. But it's bigger than that. It's the people at the bar. 

You see, I've been there a long time, right? I'm the senior guy. And over the years, I've sort of taken on this role... I don't know, almost like a mentor, I guess, to the younger kids who come in to barback or learn the ropes. I trained half the staff we have right now. And we also have this back room, this sort of unused space that I convinced the owner to let me use to host local artists, you know, give them a place to hang their stuff, maybe sell a few pieces on a busy Friday night. I promised them I'd manage it, curate it, make it a real thing for them. 

But now... with my head so messed up, I can't even remember to order the right garnishes, let alone coordinate an art show or teach a new kid how to properly balance a cocktail menu. I just... I look at them, these young bartenders looking to me for guidance, or these artists who trusted me with their work, and I just know I'm completely letting them down. I'm failing them. I promised them space, I promised them help, and I'm just ruining it. I'm wrecking their shot at getting noticed, or learning a trade, because I can't even keep my own brain functioning. 

And the worst part is... I keep thinking that I deserve it. Whatever happens to me, however bad this gets, I deserve it for letting all those people down. I made promises I can't keep, and now they're the ones paying the price for my... my whatever this is. My failure. So yeah, burden doesn't even begin to cover it. I feel like I'm actively dragging everyone around me down into the mud with me.
Do you feel like you're unable to initiate or continue activities due to a lack of energy or motivation?

Energy... yeah. I mean, I still do the things, because I have to, right? Like I said before, the muscle memory takes over and I go through the motions at the same speed. But the actual energy it takes to keep that engine running? It's completely shot. It's just... it's gone. 

Take the start of my shift, for example. Usually, I get in around three or four in the afternoon, depending on the day, and the very first thing you have to do before the doors open is restock the bar from the night before. You go down to the liquor room, take inventory of what's empty, and haul the replacement bottles up the stairs. It's standard prep work. I've done it ten thousand times. But lately... man, by the time I carry a couple cases of liquor up those stairs, or even just set up the service well—you know, filling the ice bins, cutting the limes and lemons, getting the speed rail organized—my body feels like I've already worked a double. 

And the crazy thing is, that's before we even unlock the front doors for the customers. I could have done absolutely nothing all morning. I could have just sat in that recliner I told you about, staring at the wall, barely lifting a finger all day at the house, so you'd think I'd be rested. But even if I barely did anything that day, just doing that basic thirty-minute setup completely wipes me out. It feels like I just worked a fourteen-hour New Year's Eve shift, and my night hasn't even started yet. 

I used to be able to do all that prep, work a packed Friday night, close down the bar, scrub the mats, and still have the energy to grab a beer with the kitchen staff at two in the morning. Now, I bring up two boxes of vodka and a case of tequila, and I feel like my bones are made of lead. The exhaustion is just so deep. I just want to lay down right there on the sticky rubber floor behind the bar and not get up. I still push through it, because I have a job to do and I'm already letting enough people down, but... yeah, the tank is just completely empty before I even get out of first gear. It takes everything I have just to keep standing there.
Do you feel like you're moving more quickly or slowly than usual when you're not at work?

Honestly... I couldn't really tell you if the actual speed of my walking or whatever is any different. Because, well, like I was telling you before about that recliner in the living room, when I'm not at the bar, I'm just not doing a whole lot of moving in the first place. 

You know, we have this small ranch house, and the layout is pretty tight. It's maybe fifteen, twenty steps tops from my chair to the kitchen sink. If I get up to get a glass of water, or if I have to let the dog out in the backyard—we have this older beagle mix, Buster, and he needs to go out a couple times a day—I just get up and do it. I walk to the back door, I turn the knob, I wait for him. I don't feel like I'm moving in slow motion, like in some movie, you know? I don't feel like I'm wading through molasses or anything like that. And I'm definitely not zooming around the house either. 

Like, if my wife asks me to take the trash out to the curb on Tuesday nights... we live on this quiet cul-de-sac, so it's a bit of a walk down the driveway to get to the street. And I'll get up, tie the bag off, walk it down there... and it's just a normal walk, I guess? I mean, I haven't noticed that it takes me any longer to get to the end of the driveway than it used to. I just do the task, whatever small thing it is, at a regular, everyday pace, and then I go right back inside and sit back down. 

So, yeah, I really haven't noticed any change in how fast or slow I'm actually moving. The speed of my legs or my arms, it's just normal, I suppose. It's just that I don't have the drive to get up and do the moving very often. But when I do, the speed is just the same as it always was.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual when you're doing everyday activities at home?

Well, like I was kind of getting at just a second ago... no, I really don't think so. The actual physical speed of what I'm doing at home hasn't changed at all. It's just the amount of time I spend actually doing things that's dropped off a cliff. 

When I'm actually up and doing some everyday chore around the house—which, again, isn't often because I'm usually just anchored to that recliner—I'm moving at a completely normal pace. Like yesterday afternoon, for instance. I finally got up to make myself a sandwich. Just some turkey and Swiss, nothing fancy, but I had to get the mayo from the back of the fridge, grab the bread from the pantry, get a knife out of the block... and the whole time I was doing it, I wasn't moving like a zombie, you know? I was just making a sandwich. Opening the jars, spreading the mayo, putting the cheese on... all at the exact same speed I would have done it five years ago. 

Or take doing the dishes. We don't have a dishwasher, so it's all by hand, and we don't have a huge sink either, so you gotta wash a few, dry a few, put 'em on the drying rack so they don't pile up. When I'm standing there with the sponge, my hands are moving just fine. I'm not scrubbing the plates in slow motion, I'm not taking ten minutes to rinse a single coffee mug. I just wash them. 

So it's not the physical speed of my arms or my legs that's the problem. I'm not shuffling my feet down the hallway or moving like an old man with a walker. doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation to differentiate between F32.0, F32.1, F32.2, and F32.3
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in how quickly or slowly you think, compared to before you started feeling this way?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: Inventory used to be automatic for me, but now I stare at the bottles and lose count three times, or I freeze trying to decide something simple like what garnish to restock.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in the speed of my thinking, which relates to my diminished ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I have. It's... it's honestly like my brain is trying to walk through wet concrete these days. Everything is just so incredibly slow. You know, I've been doing this job for a long time, and a lot of the mental work used to just be completely automatic for me. Take inventory, for example. I used to be able to walk into the liquor room with my clipboard, scan the shelves, and just knock it out in ten minutes flat. I knew exactly what we had, what we were moving, what we needed to order from the distributor before they even called. It was second nature. 

But now? I go back there to do the counts, and I just stand there staring at the bottles. I'll start counting the well vodka or the bourbons, and I'll get to maybe four or five, and then my mind just completely blanks. I'll lose count three times on the exact same shelf. I just lose the thread of what I'm doing. It's like the gears in my head are rusted shut. 

And it's not even just the big tasks like the weekly liquor order. It's the stupid, tiny things that really show me how bad it's gotten. When I'm setting up my station before a shift, you know, getting the fruit caddies ready... I'll just freeze trying to decide something incredibly simple, like what garnish to restock first. I'll be standing there looking at the cutting board, holding a paring knife, and I can't figure out if I should slice the limes or pull out the cocktail cherries. It's a choice that shouldn't take even a fraction of a second, but I'll just stand there, totally paralyzed, trying to force my brain to make a decision. The processing speed is just gone. I used to be so sharp, calculating tabs in my head, remembering a dozen drink orders at once, but now I can barely figure out how to restock a lemon without my brain just shutting down on me.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving slower or more slowly than you used to, physically?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical slowness or psychomotor retardation, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Physically? Moving slow... no, I wouldn't say that. It's funny you ask, because you'd think with my head being so bogged down and foggy like I was just saying, my body would naturally follow suit, but... no. It doesn't. 

That muscle memory I was talking about earlier with talking to customers? It applies to my feet and my hands, too. You see, behind a bar, especially a high-volume place like ours on a weekend, space is incredibly tight. You've got maybe three feet, tops, between the speed rail and the backbar coolers, and you're constantly weaving around the other bartender, the barbacks hauling ice, the waitresses coming up to the service well to grab their tickets. It's essentially a dance. The "bartender's shuffle," some of the old-timers call it. And I've been doing that exact dance for so many years that my body just inherently knows the tempo. Two steps left to the ice bin, pivot on the right foot, grab the shaker tin, reach down for the well rail... it's all entirely on physical autopilot. 

I can still sling drinks and wipe down the mahogany just as fast as I always have. I can still haul a fifty-pound keg from the walk-in cooler and tap it without missing a beat, or scrub down the three-compartment sink at the end of the night at my usual pace. It's actually a very strange, almost disconnected feeling, to be completely honest with you. My body is moving at its normal clip, my hands are shaking a margarita or pouring a draft just as quick as they did ten years ago, but inside? Inside, I feel like I'm completely hollowed out. 

But outwardly, physically... no, my wife hasn't mentioned me walking any slower around the house, and I certainly haven't noticed it taking me any longer to walk the four blocks from the train station to the front doors of the bar every afternoon. My legs and arms work at the exact same speed they always have. It's just... the engine running them is completely exhausted, you know? But the actual physical movement itself hasn't slowed down a bit.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation to differentiate between F32.0, F32.1, F32.2, and F32.3
doctor.question: Do you find yourself fidgeting or feeling like you need to move around when you're sitting still?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation (fidgeting, restlessness), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Fidgeting? No, not at all. If anything, it’s the exact opposite. When I actually get a chance to sit down, I just stay there. Like a sack of wet sand. 

You know, in my line of work, you’re on your feet for eight, ten, twelve hours a shift on the hard rubber mats behind the bar. The only time I really get to sit is if I take a quick ten-minute breather out back by the dumpsters on an old plastic milk crate, or when I finally get home at three in the morning and collapse into the recliner in the living room. And when I hit that chair, I don't tap my foot. I don't bounce my knee or pick at my fingernails or pace around the room. I just sink into the cushions and stay completely still. 

My wife, she’ll be sitting on the sofa reading or watching her shows, and I’ll just be sitting there in the dark, staring at the wall next to the television. I don't feel any urge whatsoever to get up and move. I don't have that kind of nervous, jittery energy. Like I was saying before about the tank being completely empty... fidgeting takes energy, you know? It takes a kind of spark or a restlessness that I just absolutely do not have in me right now. 

I can sit at the kitchen table with a mug of coffee, completely zone out, and the coffee will go ice cold before I even shift my weight in the chair. I could sit in the exact same spot for hours without moving a single muscle, just letting all these heavy, awful thoughts I’ve been having just wash over me. So no, I don't get fidgety. When I stop moving, I just... stop completely.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're a burden to your wife or others around you?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I let down the younger bartenders and the artists I promised space to, and it feels like I deserve whatever happens to me for wrecking their shot.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient feels like a burden, which assesses feelings of worthlessness or guilt.

patient.answer:
Yeah. Yeah, I do. All the time, honestly. It's... it's heavy. It's this weight I carry around with me, and it's not just about my wife, though I know I'm no picnic to live with right now, just sitting in that recliner like a lump like I told you. But it's bigger than that. It's the people at the bar. 

You see, I've been there a long time, right? I'm the senior guy. And over the years, I've sort of taken on this role... I don't know, almost like a mentor, I guess, to the younger kids who come in to barback or learn the ropes. I trained half the staff we have right now. And we also have this back room, this sort of unused space that I convinced the owner to let me use to host local artists, you know, give them a place to hang their stuff, maybe sell a few pieces on a busy Friday night. I promised them I'd manage it, curate it, make it a real thing for them. 

But now... with my head so messed up, I can't even remember to order the right garnishes, let alone coordinate an art show or teach a new kid how to properly balance a cocktail menu. I just... I look at them, these young bartenders looking to me for guidance, or these artists who trusted me with their work, and I just know I'm completely letting them down. I'm failing them. I promised them space, I promised them help, and I'm just ruining it. I'm wrecking their shot at getting noticed, or learning a trade, because I can't even keep my own brain functioning. 

And the worst part is... I keep thinking that I deserve it. Whatever happens to me, however bad this gets, I deserve it for letting all those people down. I made promises I can't keep, and now they're the ones paying the price for my... my whatever this is. My failure. So yeah, burden doesn't even begin to cover it. I feel like I'm actively dragging everyone around me down into the mud with me.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to initiate or continue activities due to a lack of energy or motivation?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By the time I carry a couple cases of liquor or set up the well, my body feels like I've already worked a double, even if I barely did anything that day.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about a lack of energy or motivation to initiate or continue activities, which aligns directly with the symptom of fatigue.

patient.answer:
Energy... yeah. I mean, I still do the things, because I have to, right? Like I said before, the muscle memory takes over and I go through the motions at the same speed. But the actual energy it takes to keep that engine running? It's completely shot. It's just... it's gone. 

Take the start of my shift, for example. Usually, I get in around three or four in the afternoon, depending on the day, and the very first thing you have to do before the doors open is restock the bar from the night before. You go down to the liquor room, take inventory of what's empty, and haul the replacement bottles up the stairs. It's standard prep work. I've done it ten thousand times. But lately... man, by the time I carry a couple cases of liquor up those stairs, or even just set up the service well—you know, filling the ice bins, cutting the limes and lemons, getting the speed rail organized—my body feels like I've already worked a double. 

And the crazy thing is, that's before we even unlock the front doors for the customers. I could have done absolutely nothing all morning. I could have just sat in that recliner I told you about, staring at the wall, barely lifting a finger all day at the house, so you'd think I'd be rested. But even if I barely did anything that day, just doing that basic thirty-minute setup completely wipes me out. It feels like I just worked a fourteen-hour New Year's Eve shift, and my night hasn't even started yet. 

I used to be able to do all that prep, work a packed Friday night, close down the bar, scrub the mats, and still have the energy to grab a beer with the kitchen staff at two in the morning. Now, I bring up two boxes of vodka and a case of tequila, and I feel like my bones are made of lead. The exhaustion is just so deep. I just want to lay down right there on the sticky rubber floor behind the bar and not get up. I still push through it, because I have a job to do and I'm already letting enough people down, but... yeah, the tank is just completely empty before I even get out of first gear. It takes everything I have just to keep standing there.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more quickly or slowly than usual when you're not at work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor agitation or retardation (moving more quickly or slowly than usual), which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Honestly... I couldn't really tell you if the actual speed of my walking or whatever is any different. Because, well, like I was telling you before about that recliner in the living room, when I'm not at the bar, I'm just not doing a whole lot of moving in the first place. 

You know, we have this small ranch house, and the layout is pretty tight. It's maybe fifteen, twenty steps tops from my chair to the kitchen sink. If I get up to get a glass of water, or if I have to let the dog out in the backyard—we have this older beagle mix, Buster, and he needs to go out a couple times a day—I just get up and do it. I walk to the back door, I turn the knob, I wait for him. I don't feel like I'm moving in slow motion, like in some movie, you know? I don't feel like I'm wading through molasses or anything like that. And I'm definitely not zooming around the house either. 

Like, if my wife asks me to take the trash out to the curb on Tuesday nights... we live on this quiet cul-de-sac, so it's a bit of a walk down the driveway to get to the street. And I'll get up, tie the bag off, walk it down there... and it's just a normal walk, I guess? I mean, I haven't noticed that it takes me any longer to get to the end of the driveway than it used to. I just do the task, whatever small thing it is, at a regular, everyday pace, and then I go right back inside and sit back down. 

So, yeah, I really haven't noticed any change in how fast or slow I'm actually moving. The speed of my legs or my arms, it's just normal, I suppose. It's just that I don't have the drive to get up and do the moving very often. But when I do, the speed is just the same as it always was.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual when you're doing everyday activities at home?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving more slowly than usual), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was kind of getting at just a second ago... no, I really don't think so. The actual physical speed of what I'm doing at home hasn't changed at all. It's just the amount of time I spend actually doing things that's dropped off a cliff. 

When I'm actually up and doing some everyday chore around the house—which, again, isn't often because I'm usually just anchored to that recliner—I'm moving at a completely normal pace. Like yesterday afternoon, for instance. I finally got up to make myself a sandwich. Just some turkey and Swiss, nothing fancy, but I had to get the mayo from the back of the fridge, grab the bread from the pantry, get a knife out of the block... and the whole time I was doing it, I wasn't moving like a zombie, you know? I was just making a sandwich. Opening the jars, spreading the mayo, putting the cheese on... all at the exact same speed I would have done it five years ago. 

Or take doing the dishes. We don't have a dishwasher, so it's all by hand, and we don't have a huge sink either, so you gotta wash a few, dry a few, put 'em on the drying rack so they don't pile up. When I'm standing there with the sponge, my hands are moving just fine. I'm not scrubbing the plates in slow motion, I'm not taking ten minutes to rinse a single coffee mug. I just wash them. 

So it's not the physical speed of my arms or my legs that's the problem. I'm not shuffling my feet down the hallway or moving like an old man with a walker. It's just that getting the engine to turn over and actually *start* doing those everyday things takes a miracle. The motivation is completely dead. But once I'm finally up and forced to do the thing? No, I'm moving just as fast as I ever did.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of interest in activities they once enjoyed for more than two weeks
doctor.question: Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy for more than two weeks?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I came in because nothing feels like mine anymore—I used to get excited about murals, runs, basketball, even making a good drink, and now I just stand there like I don't care about any of it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest in activities I used to enjoy, which matches my symptom of losing interest in things like murals, runs, basketball, and making good drinks.

patient.answer:
Yeah, way more than two weeks. Honestly, it's been going on for a long time now, and that's... well, that's really the main reason I finally came in to see somebody. Because nothing feels like mine anymore, if that makes any sense. It's like I'm just renting space in my own life. 

I used to have all these things that I really looked forward to, things that made me feel like me. Like, I used to get so excited about painting murals. Just local community stuff, you know? Down by the old train overpass or on the side of some of the local businesses on Main Street that wanted a little color on their brick walls. I'd spend hours at the kitchen table just sketching out designs, figuring out the colors, and I'd get totally lost in it. It was my release. 

And I used to love going for long runs, too. I'd get up early, before the sun was even fully up and the neighborhood was still dead quiet, and just hit the pavement. Or basketball—I had this regular pickup game every Sunday morning at the community center with a bunch of guys I've known since high school. We aren't exactly spring chickens anymore, but we'd go out there, sweat it out, talk trash, grab a coffee afterward. I lived for that Sunday game. 

Hell, even at work... I know I was just complaining about how exhausting the bar is now, but I actually used to genuinely enjoy my job. I used to get a real kick out of making a really good drink. Like when someone orders a proper Old Fashioned, and you take the time to muddle the sugar and bitters just right, you get the big ice cube, you express the orange peel over the glass so they get that citrus smell right before they take a sip... I used to take real pride in that. I liked seeing the customer take that first sip and give you that little nod of approval. 

But now? Man, I haven't picked up a sketchbook or a paintbrush in months. The guys text me about hoops on Sundays and I just leave them on read, or I make up some excuse about my back acting up. My running shoes are just gathering dust by the door. And at the bar, I just stand there making the drinks like a robot. I just stand there like I don't care about any of it. Because I don't. The excitement, the pride, the fun... it's just completely gone from every single thing I used to love.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of depressed mood
doctor.question: Do you feel sad most of the day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood (feeling sad), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sad? No, I wouldn't really use that word. I mean, when I think of being sad, I think of... well, like when my buddy's dad passed away a few years back. You know? That was sad. I was crying at the funeral, I felt that heavy ache in my chest, the whole nine yards. You feel a real physical reaction when you're sad. 

But what I'm dealing with right now, most of the day... it's not that. I don't sit in my recliner crying my eyes out or feeling sorry for myself. In fact, my wife asked me almost that exact same question just the other day. She came into the living room—I was just sitting there, staring at the wall, didn't even have the TV on—and she put her hand on my shoulder and asked, "Are you feeling sad today?" And I really had to think about it for a minute. 

But honestly, no. It's not sadness. Sadness feels like an actual emotion, like something is actively happening inside you. But for me, from the time I finally drag myself out of bed to the time I'm standing behind the mahogany at work, wiping down the speed rack for the hundredth time... I don't feel sad. I just don't really feel much of anything at all. It's more of a flat line. If a tearjerker movie comes on, or if I hear some tragic news on the local station, I don't get choked up. I just sort of sit there. So no, I definitely wouldn't say I feel sad most of the day. I'm just sort of... blank, I guess you could say.

doctor.question: Have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite or eating habits over the past two months?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: Most days I forget to eat until my hands start shaking behind the bar, then I might grab a few bites of something cold after closing and feel sick looking at it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant changes in appetite or eating habits, which matches the Weight_Appetite_Change symptom.

patient.answer:
Appetite... well, yeah, I guess you could say it's pretty much non-existent at this point. I just... I don't even think about food anymore. I mean, most days, I'll wake up, sit in that recliner like I told you, eventually drag myself to work... and I'll completely forget to eat a single thing. It doesn't even cross my mind. 

I won't even realize it until I'm right in the middle of a shift at the bar. I'll be reaching for a bottle of bourbon or trying to pour a draft beer, and I'll look down and my hands are just shaking. Like, literally trembling. And you can't have shaky hands when you're pouring drinks, you know? You spill, you mess up the measurements, people look at you across the mahogany like you're going through withdrawals or something. 

So that's usually the first time it hits me that my tank is completely empty. But even then, I don't stop to eat. I can't, really, it's too busy. I just push through the rest of the night. And then, finally, it's like 2:30 in the morning, the doors are locked, the floors are mopped, the registers are all counted out... and I'll go into the back room. The kitchen's been closed for hours, obviously, so I'll just open the walk-in and grab whatever's sitting around. Usually just a few bites of something cold, like a leftover chicken wrap or some cold fries from a messed-up order earlier in the night. 

But the thing is, I'll sit there under those harsh fluorescent lights in the office, take maybe one or two bites, and I just feel sick even looking at the rest of it. My stomach just totally turns. It's like looking at a plate of wet cardboard, the thought of swallowing another bite actually makes me nauseous. I end up just tossing it in the trash and going home empty. It's been like that for a while now, just... running on absolute fumes until my hands start shaking, and then feeling completely sick to my stomach when I actually try to put something in it.
